system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2181-11-02 22:14:00 to 2181-11-05 14:44:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of living donor liver transplant for primary sclerosing cholangitis presented with sudden-onset right upper quadrant abdominal pain and elevated liver enzymes. Initial imaging showed patent hepatic vasculature but no clear cause. A transjugular liver biopsy revealed mild acute cellular rejection, prompting treatment with high-dose steroids, increased immunosuppression, and valganciclovir. Despite therapy, liver enzymes continued to rise, leading to a second biopsy that showed resolution of rejection but mild steatosis. The transaminitis was attributed to medication effects, particularly Seroquel and temazepam, both of which were discontinued. Steroid-induced mood symptoms were managed with Ativan and Seroquel, but the latter was stopped due to liver concerns. The patient improved clinically, with pain control and stabilization of labs. She was discharged on a tapering steroid regimen, adjusted immunosuppression, insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, and instructions to restart clopidogrel. Follow-up was arranged for lab monitoring and outpatient evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team tonight. You came in with fever and right upper belly pain—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up yesterday morning with chills and a fever of 102. I had a headache and body aches all over. Then later, I started feeling pain in my upper right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vomiting, or changes in urine or stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. I do have a cough, but it’s been there for a while—my doctor says it’s from my blood pressure medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve run some blood tests and found your liver enzymes are elevated. That’s why we’re concerned. We’re also checking for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this another rejection episode? I had one earlier this year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one possibility, but we’re also looking at infection or a bile duct issue. Your transplant history makes both concerns important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What tests are you doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already done an ultrasound of your liver and a chest X-ray. The ultrasound shows your liver blood vessels are open and no blockage in the bile ducts. Chest is clear too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the fever and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. We’ve started antibiotics just in case it’s an infection. We’ll keep monitoring your labs and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another biopsy like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping not. If your symptoms improve and your liver tests come down, we may avoid it. We’ll reassess in the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative so far, and your fever has gone down. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The pain is almost gone, and I don’t feel achy anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your liver enzymes are already starting to improve too. This suggests it wasn’t a serious infection or rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what was it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One possibility is a small gallstone briefly blocked your bile duct and then passed. That could explain the sudden symptoms and quick recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Even though I had my gallbladder out years ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stones can still form in the bile ducts. Since you’re improving, we don’t think further intervention is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Are you still giving me antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop them later today since there’s no sign of infection. You’ll continue your regular transplant meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure medicine? I noticed it wasn’t given last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your lisinopril temporarily in case of infection, but we’ll restart it today since you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. Liver enzymes are dropping, and your white blood count is stable. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch you one more night to be safe. If all stays well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Should I be worried about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to predict, but we’ll monitor your liver tests closely. Your transplant team will want to see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs this morning are even better. Liver tests are nearly back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does this mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this afternoon. You’ll need to follow up with your liver doctor and get blood work done early next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What labs do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, and cyclosporine level. You have standing orders at your local lab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, chills, belly pain, or jaundice. Also, weigh yourself daily and call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to your usual low-salt, gluten-free diet. Stay hydrated but avoid excess fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, and we’re confident you’re recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Keep taking all your medications as prescribed and keep those follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis and prior liver transplant presented with acute fever, rigors, and right upper quadrant pain. Initial labs showed elevated liver enzymes, raising concern for infection or transplant rejection. Imaging revealed patent hepatic vasculature without biliary dilation, and blood cultures were negative. She was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for 36 hours, after which her symptoms rapidly improved and liver function tests began to normalize. Given her clinical improvement, antibiotics were discontinued and a liver biopsy was avoided. The episode was attributed to a likely transient biliary obstruction, possibly from a passed stone. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with her transplant team and complete outpatient lab monitoring.
